item.title: Eggshells-inspired aluminum material offers significant protection from space debris
item.description: There are nearly 1 million pieces of debris larger than 1 centimeter (0.4 inch) in near-Earth orbit. As we continue launching spacecraft and telescopes to explore the universe, this debris poses a significant threat of high-speed impact damage. In the Journal of Applied Physics researchers from Dalian University of Technology in China explored an eggshell-inspired design as a potential spacecraft protection material. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ask an expert: How to talk to children about 9/11
item.description: For millions of Americans, Sept. 11, 2001, is a vivid memory. For younger generations, it's a history lesson. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new game demonstrates quantum advantage with provable classical limits
item.description: For decades, physicists have worked to prove the strange predictions of quantum mechanics with real experiments. As quantum computers have grown more powerful, researchers have devised increasingly sophisticated ways to test whether these machines are truly harnessing quantum effects—but every method so far has run into limits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Compulsory grammar tests in England's schools aren't improving children's writing
item.description: For more than a decade, children in Year 6—the final year of elementary school in England—have taken the grammar, punctuation and spelling test as part of their Key Stage 2 Standard Assessment Tests (SATs). This GPS test has shaped how grammar is taught in elementary schools. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sea ice creates hidden highways for young Antarctic krill
item.description: New research shows that larval Antarctic krill could be carried far from their birthplace by drifting sea ice, linking distant ecosystems in ways conventional models may miss. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How studying astronauts could help tackle aging on Earth
item.description: Astronauts who undergo long-duration spaceflight aboard the International Space Station often return with health problems that resemble some age-related conditions in people on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 1,000 Museum Visitors Dive Into NASA Sea Level Science on World Ocean Day
item.description: More than 1,000 visitors explored NASA sea level science firsthand during World Ocean Day at the University of Georgia Aquarium on Skidaway Island on June 6, 2026. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA’s Hubble, Webb Find Far-out Solar System Objects ‘Remember’ Past
item.description: For the first time, scientists used the joint power of NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes to study some of the most far-flung bodies in our solar system, Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs). Some of these are the smallest and faintest ever directly seen. The researchers unexpectedly found fewer small TNOs than they expected, and that […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Superfluid qubit could help scale up quantum computers
item.description: Superfluid helium could offer a new way to tackle one of the biggest challenges in scaling up quantum computers, say researchers from the University of Surrey. The research team has introduced a conceptual design for a new type of qubit that could be much less vulnerable to errors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a powerful new antivenom hidden in rattlesnake blood
item.description: Researchers discovered that combinations of toxin-blocking proteins naturally found in rattlesnake blood can powerfully neutralize venom from several dangerous snake species. In lab tests, the mixtures were about 10 times more potent than a current commercial antivenom, pointing toward a new generation of nature-inspired snakebite treatments. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized
item.description: More than 1,200 genetic variants have been linked to the Big Five personality traits, and many of the same variants are also associated with health, longevity, careers, income, and everyday habits. The findings reveal a surprisingly wide genetic connection between personality and life outcomes while showing that environment still plays a powerful role. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Plateau pikas, long considered pests, can help livestock eat well
item.description: Small mammals called plateau pikas are often treated as pests because they compete with livestock for food, but research from China shows they can improve the quality of vegetation for grazing yaks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A photon that challenges Einstein: According to current physics, it should never have reached Earth
item.description: How did a photon survive a journey of more than 2 billion light-years when, according to known physics, it should have been absorbed long before reaching Earth? This is the question at the heart of a new study by Giorgio Galanti (INAF) and Marco Roncadelli (INFN), accepted for publication in Physical Review Letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Big supernova dataset challenges dark energy theory
item.description: The most comprehensive catalog of exploding white dwarf stars ever assembled has revealed new clues about dark energy, the mysterious force driving the universe's accelerating expansion. Researchers at The University of Queensland's School of Mathematics and Physics have led a global effort to compile a dataset containing information on 2,884 Type Ia supernovae used to measure cosmic distances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Distracted dog walkers may be putting wildlife and livestock at risk, study finds
item.description: Dog walkers distracted by their phones, conversations or other demands can fail to notice their pets defecating, disturbing wildlife or approaching livestock, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New screening system flags food-packaging chemicals linked to serious health risks
item.description: Packaged food usually sits in plastic-lined bags designed to keep air, moisture and contaminants out. That same protection can also increase the chances of chemicals from the packaging seeping into the food. When a chemical raises health concerns, industries often swap it for a molecular cousin, a substitution that may either be genuinely safer or simply be too understudied to know whether it is harmful. With thousands of chemicals in use, one-by-one regulation can't keep pace, so untested replacements can slide through unchecked. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research: We're not protecting our oceans as well as we think
item.description: Not so long ago, we thought the ocean was an inexhaustible resource. There would always be plenty more fish in the sea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As El Niño intensifies, scientists in Chile are making a vulnerable penguin species wear copper vests, here's why
item.description: In an inspiring initiative, Chilean researchers are designing specialized vests for injured penguins, incorporating copper and zinc to expedite healing. This groundbreaking effort is focused on supporting the struggling Humboldt penguin population by preventing further injury while enhancing recovery. The vests draw on effective treatments that have proven successful for domestic animals, showcasing a creative blend of technology and compassion. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Ozempic and Wegovy may have an unexpected mental health benefit
item.description: Semaglutide, the drug behind Ozempic and Wegovy, may have benefits that extend well beyond weight loss and diabetes. In a large Swedish study of nearly 15,000 people with bipolar disorder, its use was linked to a 21% lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization. Researchers think effects on inflammation and brain-related biological pathways could help stabilize mood, though other GLP-1 drugs did not show the same association. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Giant new dinosaur discovered beneath construction site in Brazil
item.description: Scientists have identified a giant new dinosaur from Brazil that reached about 20 meters long and lived 120 million years ago. Its surprising evolutionary ties to a Spanish dinosaur suggest its ancestors crossed ancient land connections between Europe, Africa, and South America. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: In 1980, conservationists began eradicating feral sheep to restore California's Santa Cruz Island
item.description: Conservationists undertook a significant effort to remove feral sheep from Santa Cruz Island, aiming to revive its delicate ecosystem. Over seven years, thousands of these sheep were eliminated, risking the extinction of a unique heritage breed. To counter this, twelve lambs were rescued to spearhead a captive breeding initiative on the mainland, ensuring the preservation of a rare genetic lineage and honoring California's rich agricultural heritage. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Super-resolution imaging reveals details inside living cells
item.description: A new fluorescence microscopy technique that generates super-resolution images from a single camera exposure could help researchers study rapid movements within cells that are difficult to capture with existing methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Working with anglers to save England's sharks
item.description: I spent six days on a small fishing boat in the middle of the English Channel in July trying to catch a thresher shark. The weather was fickle, even at the height of summer. My colleague, ecologist Lucy Hawkes, and I were with two anglers who probably hold more experience of Channel thresher sharks than anyone alive. Between us, we caught nothing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: With another huge infusion of cash, Stoke Space goes even bigger
item.description: The space economy will grow exactly as fast as we can launch rockets. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: What students gain and lose as AI chatbots take over parts of university teaching
item.description: Universities are increasingly introducing artificial intelligence (AI) teaching tools into classrooms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists observe Einstein’s gravity in the quantum world for the first time
item.description: Physicists have directly observed a long-predicted quantum effect of gravity, putting one of Einstein’s foundational ideas to a striking new test. Using ultracold atoms, researchers split an atom’s quantum wave so that one part was held in place while the other fell freely under gravity, then reunited the two to measure the tiny difference that emerged. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: En 1984, la NASA envió 3301 abejas al espacio para ver de qué eran capaces. Siete días después habían construido 200 cm² de hexágonos
item.description: En abril de 1984, mientras cinco astronautas del Challenger se preparaban para protagonizar la primera reparación de un satélite en órbita, unos pasajeros mucho más pequeños realizaban su propio experimento . 3.301 abejas viajaron durante siete días en microgravedad para comprobar si podían organizar una colmena y, sobre todo, construir sus característicos panales cuando desaparecía algo que en la Tierra siempre habían tenido como referencia: la gravedad. El comienzo fue accidentado, pero el resultado acabó siendo sorprendente. 3.300 abejas en el espacio. El experimento viajó en la misión… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: Can what we feed farm animals directly benefit our own health?
item.description: Several chronic diseases—obesity, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers—have been linked to lifestyles and diets high in calories, based on processed foods and lacking diversity and nutritional value. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST finds extreme star-forming galaxies masquerading as faint quasars
item.description: A new study finds that two early-universe objects thought to be faint quasars are actually extraordinarily luminous galaxies powered by bursts of star formation. James Webb Space Telescope observations of the galaxies, seen when the universe was less than a billion years old, reveal signatures of extremely massive stars, including some potentially more than 200 times the mass of the sun. The paper outlining this discovery was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 18. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The American “cheetah” wasn’t a cheetah at all
item.description: The extinct “American cheetah” was not really a cheetah at all, but a puma relative with an unexpectedly flexible lifestyle. Fossils from the Yukon suggest northern populations survived partly by eating fish, possibly including salmon, while southern cats hunted on land. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 'Digital duty of care' laws will force tech platforms to look after users
item.description: The federal government has introduced draft digital duty of care legislation designed to protect Australians from online harms. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Vaccinating dogs, not people, holds key to ending rabies deaths in Kerala, India
item.description: A new study has found that expanding dog vaccination, rather than introducing routine pre-exposure vaccination for children, is the most effective and cost-effective way to eliminate rabies deaths in people in Kerala, India. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than $1 million in elephant ivory advertised online in Australia
item.description: While most Australians assume the ivory trade ended decades ago, Adelaide University research has found an active collectors' market exists online, with most listings showing no proof that the items are legal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stoke has "completed the initial closing" of a $1B Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations.
item.description: Stoke has "completed the initial closing" of a $1B Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations. TECHCRUNCH.COM Stoke Space raises another billion to rival SpaceX at re-flying rockets | TechCrunch Fuente: TechCrunch.

item.title: Scientists find a new weakness in treatment-resistant prostate cancer
item.description: Researchers have found a potential way to attack prostate cancers that evade treatment by changing their cellular identity. Combining two types of drugs reversed many of these changes and sharply slowed tumor growth in preclinical experiments, offering a possible new strategy for aggressive, treatment-resistant disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Melting Svalbard glaciers may flush ancient methane from rocks beneath the ice
item.description: Meltwater rivers flowing from Svalbard glaciers are carrying ancient methane from rocks beneath the ice into the open air, new research published in Nature Communications shows. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Super-resolution imaging reveals that cohesin prevents local mixing of compact, active genome domains
item.description: The human genome is about two meters (6.6 feet) long, yet it is folded inside a cell nucleus only about 10 micrometers in diameter. To fit into this tiny space, DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which are further organized into chromatin. For decades, chromatin has often been described in two simple forms: euchromatin, which is active, open and accessible, and heterochromatin, which is more compact and repressed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Worm's radical transformation shows metamorphosis can change the functions of cells
item.description: A squishy worm that starts its life as something of a floating head in the Pacific Ocean is changing what scientists know about metamorphosis at the cellular level. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI model decodes cell signaling fingerprints across diverse cell types
item.description: As an embryo develops from a small cluster of stem cells, those once "blank slate" cells begin to take on more specialized roles like brain, liver or muscle cells and organize themselves into three-dimensional structures such as tissues and organs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rearranged polymer chains create degradable materials with potential for stronger, tougher packaging
item.description: What if the key to making stronger, more sustainable plastics isn't changing their ingredients, but rearranging their molecules? Virginia Tech researchers have put that idea to the test, creating degradable polymers with a new molecular architecture that combines properties often difficult to achieve in one material: strength, toughness, flexibility and the ability to block oxygen. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stoke Space raises another billion to rival SpaceX at re-flying rockets
item.description: Stoke has "completed the initial closing" of a $1B Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations. Fuente: TechCrunch.

item.title: Anak Krakatau eruption by Sentinel-3
item.description: Image: Copernicus Sentinel-3 captured a plume from the eruption of Anak Krakatau on Saturday, 5 September. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Chinese scientists propose turning abandoned coal mines into underground farms
item.description: Chinese scientists have proposed developing “underground agriculture” in abandoned coal mine tunnels as part of a push to create a green, circular economy for the country’s massive mining industry. A team of researchers from Shanxi, a major coal-producing province in central China, described the idea late last month in the journal China Mining Magazine. An estimated 15,000 abandoned mines in China are expected to close by 2030. Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, these... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.description: A study finds 31 former rugby league players have been diagnosed with the degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: The Otherworldly Geology of Vasquez Rocks
item.description: Layers of sedimentary rock that jut from the Soledad Basin at surprising angles have long enthralled television and film producers, including the team behind Star Trek. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Doctors saved this rare monkey from amputation. Months later, she gave birth
item.description: A critically endangered roloway monkey has given birth just months after surgeons performed an unusual operation that saved her foot from amputation. Her new daughter, Lagertha, is an important addition to a species believed to number fewer than 2,000 in the wild. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese researchers see climate change link to glacial collapse, warn of rising disaster risks
item.description: Study finds Tibetan plateau’s glacier area fallen to 39,000 square kilometres down from 51,000 square kilometres, with more than 14,000 glacial lakes observed Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Early Earth's auroral belts may have formed a natural ion-beam reactor for prebiotic chemistry
item.description: We usually think of auroras as beautiful lights in the night sky. I see them as visible traces of a connection between the sun, Earth's magnetic field and the atmosphere. This led me to an origin-of-life question: Could the planetary structure that produces auroras also have organized chemical reactions on early Earth? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden immune signal that helps spinal cords regrow
item.description: A surprising immune system signal may help explain why zebrafish can regenerate damaged spinal cords so effectively. Researchers found that certain neutrophils release Il-4, which calms harmful inflammation and allows injured nerve fibers to grow again. Without these cells, healing stalled, but adding Il-4 restored regeneration. Scientists now want to know whether the same mechanism could someday be harnessed to improve spinal cord repair in humans. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Crime is falling—but the public doesn't feel safer, UK study finds
item.description: Crime levels are falling for most offenses across the UK—but the public doesn't necessarily feel safer. It's a human trait to focus on frightening information in the news or on social media—but it could also mean that people are more fearful about crime than they need to be. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How Indigenous Protected Areas became a vital way to protect nature in Australia
item.description: When you think of conservation in Australia, chances are you'll think of a national park. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Common dry-cleaning chemical linked to triple the risk of liver scarring
item.description: A chemical commonly used in dry cleaning and found in some household products may be an overlooked threat to liver health. Researchers found that people with detectable levels of tetrachloroethylene (PCE) in their blood were three times more likely to have significant liver fibrosis, a dangerous buildup of scar tissue that can eventually lead to liver failure or cancer. The risk climbed sharply as PCE levels increased, even after accounting for factors such as age, sex, race, education, alcohol use, and metabolic conditions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nearly 1.7 million deaths linked to second-hand smoke in 2023, study finds
item.description: More than 2.7 billion people worldwide, including 767 million children, were exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths, a Lancet study said on Tuesday. Researchers found second-hand smoke remained a major global health risk, with no safe level of exposure. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE 24

item.title: Park rangers and residents speak up to save Togo's last national park
item.description: A few years ago, I drove with an old friend from Togo, West Africa, towards the country's last remaining large protected area, Fazao-Malfakassa National Park. Our destination was the Hotel Fazao, where his uncle had once worked as a professional chef after its opening in 1980. For decades, while the park was managed by the Swiss Franz Weber Foundation (FWF), the hotel had hosted tourists from around the world who came to see elephants, monkeys, and other wildlife for which Africa is famous. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI governance model inspired by Pope Leo XIV aims to put ethics first
item.description: Researchers at the John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin (KUL) and the University of Eastern Finland have developed a new model of artificial intelligence governance inspired by the teachings of Pope Leo XIV as set out in his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. The new model is intended to ensure that AI technologies are developed and used safely, fairly and with full respect for human rights. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bumpy battery surfaces can masquerade as nanoscale ion pathways, misleading material design
item.description: A signal that appears to show ions moving inside a battery may, in fact, be an illusion caused by an uneven surface. A KAIST research team has identified the origin of this type of artifact, which can lead researchers to misinterpret what is happening inside a battery, and has developed a method to reduce it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Survey of young researchers raises concerns over future of science in U.S.
item.description: One-third of young scientists who had been planning careers in academic research changed their minds in the spring of 2025, according to a new survey. Fewer expected to remain in higher education or work in the U.S., or felt that pursuing a Ph.D. was the right decision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From strays to territory bosses: Epigenetics makes cheetahs adaptable
item.description: The findings of a new study led by the Leibniz-IZW on Namibian free-ranging cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus jubatus) demonstrate that epigenetic mechanisms might play an important role in how animals develop different phenotypes despite their low genetic diversity. The work is published in the journal Molecular Ecology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A child's first 5 years set them up for life. African study explores how to target education spending
item.description: The first five years of life lay an important foundation for children's future schooling, health and earnings. Yet over 77% of children in sub-Saharan Africa don't have access to early childhood care and education. This places them at risk of not reaching their development potential. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep biosphere has endured mountain-building and erosion over hundreds of millions of years
item.description: A new study reveals that microbial life deep within Earth has persisted and repeatedly flourished through hundreds of millions of years of mountain-building and erosion. By analyzing minerals, fluids and gases from a 2.3-kilometer-deep (1.4-mile-deep) borehole in central Sweden, researchers have uncovered episodic bursts of methane-producing life linked to major geological events that shaped Scandinavia. The paper is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The listening gap is real—how AI might help teachers bridge it
item.description: A Grade 4 teacher showed her class a video of children who walk miles barefoot to school. A hand shot up: "Why are you showing us AI slop? No way this is real." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists tagged 14,000 endangered moths with paint and glue; none turned up, and that may be good news
item.description: In a groundbreaking study, researchers have tagged over 14,000 Bogong moths in the Snowy Mountains of Australia. However, after extensive tracking efforts, none have been recaptured, suggesting potential populations larger than previously assumed. Alternatively, these moths might be utilizing undiscovered migration routes. The ongoing project remains crucial for understanding the ecology of these endangered insects. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: 'The Jungle Book' offers an unconventional tool for undergraduate economics education
item.description: Research in the International Journal of Pluralism and Economics Education argues that "The Jungle Book" can serve as an unconventional teaching tool for undergraduate economics, using the original stories by Rudyard Kipling as well as Disney film adaptations to introduce concepts ranging from scarcity and sustainability to happiness and development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Weak hydrogen bonds dethrone copper as the most stable metal binder, opening a new path for metal selection
item.description: Copper has been knocked off the top of a stability ranking it had dominated for decades. Without altering the atoms directly bonded to the metal, a KAIST research team reversed the longstanding trend in which copper generally forms the most stable complexes by tuning only the weak hydrogen bonds in its surrounding environment. The findings, which appear in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, could open new avenues for selective metal separation and recognition, as well as catalyst design. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Inexpensive blue pigment enables efficient one-step conversion of carbon dioxide to methane
item.description: A common blue pigment could help turn carbon dioxide (CO₂) from an industrial waste product into a useful fuel. A joint research team led by Tohoku University's Advanced Institute for Materials Research (WPI-AIMR), in collaboration with Hokkaido University and startup AZUL Energy, has developed a catalyst that converts CO₂ directly into methane (CH₄) with high efficiency using copper phthalocyanine, an inexpensive and readily available blue pigment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ships, ice cores and krill surveys underpin Australia's 10-year Antarctic monitoring strategy
item.description: The important role ships play in gathering scientific data in Antarctica and the Southern Ocean has been outlined at a leading Antarctic science conference in Hobart. The biennial Australian Antarctic Research Conference was held at the University of Tasmania and attracted 400 researchers from around the globe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why 'you're smart' can backfire: Young children may cheat more after ability praise
item.description: Parents and teachers might think telling kids "they're smart" is a helpful way to build self-confidence and support positive development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stripped-down LSD reveals structural features linked to hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects
item.description: University of California, Davis, researchers have stripped down LSD to the base features responsible for its hallucinogenic and therapeutic effects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New nitride semiconductor expands material options for more powerful electronics
item.description: Polar wurtzite nitride semiconductors, such as aluminum nitride (AlN) and gallium nitride (GaN), are central to modern high-power and high-frequency electronic devices because of their wide band gaps, high breakdown electric fields, and strong spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Heel-strike' may have allowed early humans to walk farther—at the cost of high-impact forces
item.description: The average person takes thousands of steps each day, instinctively walking heel-to-toe. Although they hardly register them, those consistent heel-first strides are more distinctive to humans than previously thought and allowed early hominins to walk farther and more efficiently, but at the cost of higher impact forces on bones and joints, according to a new study led by a researcher at Penn State. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Slender crystal's blue-to-yellow glow could make invisible forces visible
item.description: Applying pressure to luminescent organic crystals usually brings molecules closer together and weakens their fluorescence. Materials that instead brighten and undergo a large color change are rare, and clear design principles for achieving both responses in simple, rigid aromatic hydrocarbons have been lacking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What can a pair of underpants tell you about your vegetable garden?
item.description: This summer, 115 participants in Leiden and The Hague worked with scientists from Leiden University to investigate the soil life in their community garden plots. With mangetout peas, a taste test, a buried pair of underpants and a harvest festival, they helped scientists better understand the connection between soil, plants and people. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Neutrophil vesicles help Candida albicans evade immune-cell engulfment
item.description: The immune system is a highly sophisticated defense network designed to protect against pathogens. A research team from the Universities of Würzburg and Jena and the Leibniz Institute for Natural Product Research and Infection Biology (Leibniz-HKI) has shown that certain components of the immune system can actually help the yeast Candida albicans evade immune attack. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Yes, passing 1.5 C of global warming is cause for alarm, but not despair
item.description: The news has been full of headlines about findings from a United Nations report: The world is set to exceed the 1.5°C global warming target set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. The report has raised concerns and questions about what a 1.5°C increase could mean for our world. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reversible electric control unlocks persistent chiral phonon states
item.description: Atoms in a material are rarely still. They jiggle back and forth in collective lattice vibrations known as phonons. Their motion can also carry a rotational element: In 2023, scientists at PSI experimentally proved the existence of chiral phonons, which exhibit handedness depending on which way they rotate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New report offers lessons for preserving cultural heritage in crisis zones
item.description: The report, "Digital heritage preservation for vulnerable collections: Reflections on the Sudan Memory project history and inventory," was authored by Dr. Laura Gibson, senior lecturer in digital content management education at King's, alongside Sara El-Nager, independent researcher and editor, and Dr. Hannah Ishmael, lecturer in digital culture & race. It draws on 14 interviews conducted by El-Nager with contributors to the Sudan Memory project, the first mass digitization project ever undertaken in Sudan. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Entangled particles revive a 35-year-old test of the Standard Model
item.description: Physicists at the BESIII Collaboration have breathed new life into a decades-old test of one of the Standard Model's most important ideas, using a technique that had gone almost untouched by experimenters for 35 years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Organic farming outperforms wildflower strips on profits while both improve farm biodiversity
item.description: What makes more sense when farming wheat—strips of wildflowers along fields or organic farming? Both options provide financial support via the European Union as environmentally friendly and sustainable farming practices. An international research team, including researchers from the University of Göttingen, has compared the ecological and economic benefits of these two farming methods in fields planted with winter wheat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Can atmospheric methane removal limit peak warming?
item.description: In a new report, the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) concludes that global warming is expected to exceed 1.5°C within the next few years. This makes two questions increasingly important: how high will temperatures rise, and how long will the increase last? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Self-processing brain systems show both conservation and reorganization across primates
item.description: New in JNeurosci, Ning Liu, from the Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, explored whether brain structures for self-processing are conserved across primates, including humans, chimpanzees and macaques. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Excavations at Prado Vargas now span 140 square meters of a Neanderthal layer
item.description: The 2026 field season at Prado Vargas Cave, located in the village of Cornejo in the northern province of Burgos, Spain, within the Ojo Guareña karst complex, has expanded the excavation of Neanderthal sublevel 4D by 32 square meters (344 square feet), bringing the total excavated area to 140 square meters (1,507 square feet). More than 1,500 animal remains and stone tools were recovered, strengthening the interpretation of this roughly 46,000-year-old layer as a large Neanderthal camp. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could bats self-medicate? More than 50 wild bats offer clues
item.description: When humans get sick, we change our routines and try various solutions to feel better and get well, like staying in bed to rest, going to the doctor, getting medication from the pharmacy, using home remedies and more. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dark plasma regions reveal overlooked source of reactive atomic oxygen
item.description: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have found a way to make plasma more effective for its wide-ranging uses, from antimicrobial applications to surface conditioning in the semiconductor industry. They mapped the production of atomic oxygen, a key ingredient of oxygen plasma, while a high voltage was applied across oxygen gas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Galileo, Copernicus, Cleansky, IRIS² must work together to secure Europe's place in the space race
item.description: "Seeing the Earth from above is a powerful reminder of our interdependence," said Thomas Pesquet. The words of France's 10th astronaut to head into space are a reminder of how we are "in this together," something the world's aerospace industry players should take heed of as they gather in Paris for the first International Space Summit from Sept. 9–10. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fascinating read on how ancient societies handled natural hazards. So much we can still learn from how they built to adapt and recover, especially with climate extremes today…
item.description: Fascinating read on how ancient societies handled natural hazards. So much we can still learn from how they built to adapt and recover, especially with climate extremes today. That view of the Roman Forum really puts it in perspective. Shakil Ahmed Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Tiny polymer particles keep water jets stable for longer
item.description: Tiny, soft polymer particles—known as microgels—can help to stabilize extremely thin liquid jets. How this works is the finding of a study led by researchers at TU Darmstadt, which has been published in Nature Communications. The findings could be of interest for the development of needle-free medical injection systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The DESI legacy imaging survey releases the largest 2D map of the universe
item.description: In 2012, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) was commissioned to measure the effect of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the expansion of the cosmos. Since then, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys have obtained optical images of tens of millions of galaxies and quasars, including through NOIRLab's Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). In recent news, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team made its 11th data release (DR 11), constituting the largest-ever 2D map of the universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pair of white dwarfs locked in 6-minute orbit might one day be observed by gravitational waves
item.description: Current gravitational-wave observatories aren't sensitive enough to capture the gravitational waves of binary stars. They can only see the gravitational chirps of black holes just as they are merging. But that will change as more sensitive instruments are developed. Recently, a team of astronomers discovered a binary white dwarf system that could be a good target for advanced gravitational-wave observatories. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New model measures economic risks solar storms pose to US power grid
item.description: In 1967, a solar storm nearly triggered World War III by jamming early-warning radar systems in the United States, causing U.S. leaders to think the Soviet Union was responsible. Though society averted catastrophe thanks to timely information from solar forecasters, the threat from space weather remains real. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A vital native bee highway can start in your own backyard
item.description: When it comes to bees, most of us can identify the ubiquitous honey bee (Apis mellifera) and that's about it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How 'hyperselection' is making modern life efficient, pleasant—and boring
item.description: It's difficult to imagine a song like Queen's 1975 "Bohemian Rhapsody" topping the charts today. Almost six minutes long, it moves through several radically different musical sections and famously ignores the conventional structure of a pop song. It seems almost designed to break the rules of what a hit single should be. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two-color X-ray pulses capture the same nanoparticle at two moments in time
item.description: One big dream of ultrafast science has been to watch changes in nanoparticles or biomolecules on their natural timescale. Experimentally, this can be realized by taking two snapshots of the same object only femtoseconds apart. However, no detector is fast enough to record the two snapshots separately—they end up on top of each other in a single image. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: We teach students how to argue. But are we teaching them how to listen?
item.description: Picture a senior English classroom. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reconstructed ancient protein maps how bacterial enzymes evolved distinct functions
item.description: How do related proteins develop different functions? This is the question investigated by a research team involving Kiel University, DESY and the Center for Structural Systems Biology (CSSB). Led by Holger Sondermann, professor at Kiel University and head of the Structural Microbiology group at DESY, the researchers reconstructed the common ancestor of two bacterial enzymes and produced the long-extinct protein in the laboratory. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New blending method gives common polymers a visible, reversible stress signal
item.description: Polymeric materials, such as plastics and rubbers, are essential in everyday life. However, detecting where mechanical stress is concentrated inside them remains a challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What happens when you flush? Study reveals how toilet aerosols reach the breathing zone
item.description: Researchers from Flinders University have found that flushing toilets can release aerosols and bioaerosols into the surrounding air, with some studies detecting particles at heights corresponding to adults' breathing zones. Fuente: Phys.org.
